## Introduction

A GPU has one block of memory, shared by everything that runs on it: your R
session, another R session, a Python notebook, the desktop. cuplyr allocates a
lot of short-lived columns while it runs a pipeline, and *how* it asks the
driver for that memory decides three things: how fast each call is, how much of
the card cuplyr still holds after you dropped a table, and how much is left for
the other processes.

This vignette explains the three ways cuplyr can allocate (`async`, the
default; `pool`; and plain `cuda`), how to switch, how to read what cuplyr
holds, when memory is actually freed, and how to choose. It ends with numbers
measured on one machine.

```{r setup}
library(cuplyr)
library(dplyr)
```

## The three resources

cuplyr installs one RMM *memory resource* when it loads. Every GPU allocation in
the R process then goes through it.

| Resource | What it is | Speed per allocation | Memory after you drop a table | Sharing the card |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `"async"` (default) | CUDA's stream-ordered allocator (`cudaMallocAsync`) | Fast, the same as the pool by default (measured below) | Cached for reuse, like the pool, until `gpu_gc()`, which returns all of it; with the opt-in `cuplyr.release_threshold`, CUDA also returns it by itself | Good: `gpu_gc()` hands back what you dropped, and other processes can use it |
| `"pool"` | RMM's pool: one big reservation that carves out columns | Fast | Kept until the R session ends; the pool never shrinks | Poor: the card stays as full as your largest moment |
| `"cuda"` | No resource: a plain `cudaMalloc`/`cudaFree` per column | Slowest | Goes back to the device when the table is garbage collected | Good, but every allocation pays the driver |

With `async`, cuplyr reserves `cuplyr.pool_initial` bytes at load (default: a
quarter of the free device memory, at most 1 GiB) so the first calls need no
driver allocation. After that the async pool grows when a pipeline needs more
and, by default, **keeps what it grew to**, ready for the next call. That is
what makes it as fast as the pool. Unlike the pool, it can give the memory back:
`gpu_gc()` synchronises the device and returns everything the async pool holds
unused, so a pipeline that briefly needed 6 GB does not have to hold 6 GB for
the rest of the session.

### Automatic release (opt-in)

If you want the memory back without calling `gpu_gc()`, set
`cuplyr.release_threshold` (bytes). It is CUDA's *release threshold* for the
async pool. Whenever the GPU is synchronised, CUDA returns unused memory to the
device until the pool's **whole reservation is at or below the threshold**. The
reservation counts the tables you hold and the results R has not collected yet,
not just the cached part. That has a cost: while your session holds more than
the threshold, nothing freed stays cached, and every allocation goes to the
driver again, at about the speed of plain `cudaMalloc`. A threshold of `0` keeps
nothing at all, the "share the card" setting. Synchronisations are not limited
to `collect()`, `print()` and `gpu_sync()`; libcudf also synchronises inside many
calls (for example whenever it copies a size or a count back to the host), so a
release can happen in the middle of a pipeline. The `release_threshold = 0`
column of the table at the end of this vignette shows the price on this
machine.

## Switching resources

The resource is chosen **when the package loads**, and there is one resource per
R process. To change it, restart R. Set the switch before `library(cuplyr)`.

| What | Option | Environment variable |
|---|---|---|
| Kind of resource: `"async"` (default), `"pool"`, or `"cuda"`/`"none"` for no resource | `cuplyr.memory_resource` | `CUPLYR_MEMORY_RESOURCE` |
| Turn the resource off (`"cuda"`): `FALSE`, `"0"`, `"false"`, `"no"`, `"off"` | `cuplyr.memory_pool` | `CUPLYR_MEMORY_POOL` |
| How much the resource reserves at load, in bytes (not a limit) | `cuplyr.pool_initial` | `CUPLYR_POOL_INITIAL` |
| Async only: release unused memory automatically while the whole reservation is above this many bytes | `cuplyr.release_threshold` | `CUPLYR_RELEASE_THRESHOLD` |

An option wins over its environment variable. Case and surrounding blanks do
not matter. An unknown kind (say `"managed"`) is not silently accepted: cuplyr
warns, naming the option or variable and the value as you typed it, and uses
`"async"`; if `cuplyr.memory_pool` switches the resource off, the warning says
the kind is ignored and no resource (`"cuda"`) is used. A
`cuplyr.release_threshold` option that is `NA` or `""` counts as unset (the
environment variable decides); any other value that is not a non-negative
number warns the same way and means no automatic release. The release threshold
is ignored under `"pool"` and `"cuda"`.

Where the GPU or driver does not support `cudaMallocAsync`, the async resource
cannot be created. If async was only the default (nothing chosen, or an unknown
kind), cuplyr installs `"pool"` instead and warns. If you asked for `"async"` by
name, it warns and installs nothing (`"cuda"`).

```{r switch, eval = FALSE}
# In a fresh R session, before loading cuplyr:
options(cuplyr.memory_resource = "pool")   # the pool instead of async
# or: options(cuplyr.memory_resource = "cuda")  # plain cudaMalloc; same as
#     options(cuplyr.memory_pool = FALSE)
# or: options(cuplyr.release_threshold = 0)      # async: keep nothing cached
library(cuplyr)
```

From a shell, `CUPLYR_MEMORY_RESOURCE=pool Rscript script.R` does the same.
`cuplyr.release_threshold = 0` under `async` is the "share the card" setting:
unused memory goes back to the device at every synchronisation, at the price of
asking the driver for memory again on the next call.
`cuplyr.pool_initial = 0` only skips the reservation at load; the pool still
grows and caches as it needs.

## Reading the numbers

`gpu_memory_state()` reports the device and what cuplyr's resource holds:

```{r state}
st <- gpu_memory_state()
st$resource
c(free = st$free_bytes, pool = st$pool_bytes, in_use = st$pool_used_bytes)
```

* `free_bytes` (and `used_bytes`, `total_bytes`) are **device level**, for every
  process on the card. They are what `nvidia-smi` shows. `used_bytes` includes
  the memory the resource holds for reuse, so freeing a table does not lower it
  while the resource keeps the memory: never under `"pool"`, and under `"async"`
  only after `gpu_gc()` or an automatic release has handed the memory back.
* `pool_bytes` is what cuplyr's resource currently holds from the device (the
  pool's size, or the async pool's reservation).
* `pool_used_bytes` is what cuplyr is actually using: bytes allocated to live
  columns and scratch space. It rises when you create a table and falls when the
  table is garbage collected, under both resources.
* Under `"cuda"` there is no resource, so `pool_bytes` and `pool_used_bytes` are
  `NA` and `free_bytes` is the whole truth.

So to ask "how big are my tables?" read `pool_used_bytes`; to ask "how much of
the card am I taking from others?" read `pool_bytes` (or `free_bytes`).

```{r usage}
gpu_df <- tbl_gpu(data.frame(x = runif(1e6)), lazy = FALSE)
gpu_memory_usage(gpu_df)  # estimate from dimensions and types
gpu_memory_state()$pool_used_bytes
```

`gpu_memory_usage()` estimates a table's size from its row count and column
types without touching the device. Tables that share columns (a `select()` of a
table) overlap in this estimate.

## When is memory freed?

1. **A call frees its own intermediates.** A lazy table (the default) holds
   nothing for its pending steps. An eager verb, `compute()`,
   `collect()` or `bind_rows()` releases the temporary tables its steps built
   (casts, temp columns, uploads of a data frame argument) when it returns.
2. **What you hold lives until R's garbage collector runs.** A table you
   created and dropped (`rm(gpu_df)`) is freed when R collects it. R does not
   know about GPU memory pressure, so this can be late.
3. **`gpu_gc()` forces the collection** and, under `async`, then synchronises
   and returns all unused memory of the async pool to the device (the next
   calls then grow the pool again, which costs the first call a few percent, so
   do not put it in a timing loop). It returns a
   list; `freed_bytes` is the drop in `pool_used_bytes` (what cuplyr stopped
   using) and `released_bytes` is the drop in `pool_bytes` (what went back to
   the device). `released_bytes` is 0 under `"pool"`, which cannot shrink, and
   `NA` under `"cuda"`. If the device is in a CUDA error state, `gpu_gc()`
   warns instead of failing.
4. **Out of memory.** When a GPU step fails for lack of device memory, cuplyr
   runs `gc()` and `gpu_gc(aggressive = FALSE)` itself and retries the step
   once. If it fails again you get an error of class `cuplyr_error_gpu_oom`.

```{r gc}
rm(gpu_df)
res <- gpu_gc()
c(freed = res$freed_bytes, released = res$released_bytes)
```

## How to choose

* **Leave the default (`async`)** unless you have a reason. By default it is
  as fast as the pool, and you can hand its memory back with `gpu_gc()`.
* **Use `"pool"`** only when cuplyr is the only user of the card. It is as
  fast as the default, but it never gives memory back to anyone else, not even
  after `gpu_gc()`. (Released cuplyr versions up to 0.1.1 had no resource at
  all, i.e. `"cuda"`.)
* **Use `"cuda"`** (`cuplyr.memory_resource = "cuda"` or
  `cuplyr.memory_pool = FALSE`) to debug memory: device free memory is then
  exactly what you hold. Expect slower calls.
* **Sharing the card?** Stay on `async` and call `gpu_gc()` after a large job.
  If you cannot do that, set `cuplyr.release_threshold` to the amount you are
  willing to keep reserved. Choose it above the memory your session holds when
  it works (live tables plus results R has not collected yet): below that, the
  session allocates from the driver on every call and runs at about the speed
  of `"cuda"`. `0` is the extreme of this: it keeps nothing.
* **Bigger than memory?** None of the resources makes data larger than the card
  fit; they only change how much is held on the side.

## Measured on this machine

Measured on 2026-10-23 with cuplyr 0.1.1.9000 on an RTX 5070 (12 GB). Each
number is the median of 3 fresh R processes per configuration (one resource per
process). Nothing is timed while this vignette builds; the table is static.

The four columns are `async` as shipped (no automatic release), `async` with
`cuplyr.release_threshold = 0`, `pool`, and `cuda` (no resource).

Per-call time is the median over batches of calls (after warm-up), with a GPU
synchronisation at the end of each batch:

* *small eager mutate*: `mutate(z = x * 2 + y)` on an eager 1000-row table;
* *1e6-row lazy pipeline*: `filter()`, `mutate()`, `group_by()`, `summarise()`
  and `collect()` on a lazy 1e6-row table;
* *25M-row workflow*: the README benchmark's complete workflow (`filter()`,
  `mutate()`, `group_by()`, `summarise()`, `collect()`) on a lazy table of 25
  million rows and 6 columns, about 1 GB on the GPU.

Held memory is device free memory at the starting point minus device free
memory afterwards. The starting point is taken after a `gpu_gc()` and before the
table exists. For a 1 GB and a 3 GB table, "after gc + sync" is after dropping
the table, running R's `gc()` and a synchronisation, and "after `gpu_gc()`" is
after that call.

| Measurement | `async` | `async`, `release_threshold = 0` | `pool` | `cuda` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Small eager mutate (ms per call) | 0.85 | 0.86 | 0.84 | 0.87 |
| 1e6-row lazy pipeline (ms per call) | 3.3 | 3.5 | 3.3 | 4.1 |
| 25M-row workflow (ms per call) | 14.3 | 19.0 | 14.3 | 18.0 |
| 1 GB table dropped, extra memory held after gc + sync (GB) | 1.01 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 |
| 1 GB table, after `gpu_gc()` (GB) | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 |
| 3 GB table dropped, extra memory held after gc + sync (GB) | 3.02 | 0.00 | 4.29 | 0.00 |
| 3 GB table, after `gpu_gc()` (GB) | 0.00 | 0.00 | 4.29 | 0.00 |
| Held by the resource after `gpu_gc()`, 1 GB run (GB) | 0.00 | 0.00 | 4.29 | n/a (no resource) |

The held rows are *extra* device memory, on top of the starting point. The last
row is `pool_bytes` from `gpu_memory_state()` after the 1 GB run's `gpu_gc()`.

Reading the table:

* `async` as shipped and `pool` run at the same speed (0.85 vs 0.84 ms, 3.3 vs
  3.3 ms, 14.3 vs 14.3 ms on 25M rows). Plain `cuda` is slower: 4.1 ms at 1e6
  rows and 18.0 ms at 25M rows, about 25 % more on the large workflow.
* `async` with `release_threshold = 0` keeps nothing after a synchronisation, but
  pays for it on the large workflow (19.0 ms, about a third slower than the
  default, like `cuda`) and a little at 1e6 rows (3.5 ms): every call allocates
  from the driver again.
* Default `async`: a dropped table stays cached (1.01 GB and 3.02 GB) until
  `gpu_gc()`, which returns all of it (0.00).
* `pool`: the measurements run in order in one process, and by the held-memory
  steps the 25M-row workflow had already grown the pool to 4.29 GB. The 1 GB
  table fitted inside that, so no extra memory. The 3 GB table made the pool
  grow by another 4.29 GB (it grows in large steps), which it keeps even after
  `gpu_gc()`: the pool never shrinks during the session.
* `cuda`: memory is back as soon as R has collected the table.

To repeat the measurement, run the code below once per configuration, each in a
fresh session started with `CUPLYR_MEMORY_RESOURCE=async`,
`CUPLYR_MEMORY_RESOURCE=async CUPLYR_RELEASE_THRESHOLD=0`,
`CUPLYR_MEMORY_RESOURCE=pool`, or `CUPLYR_MEMORY_POOL=0` (the resource cannot
change inside a session), and take the median of a few runs.

```{r measure, eval = FALSE}
library(cuplyr)
library(dplyr)

# Median seconds per call over `samples` batches of `reps` calls.
per_call <- function(fn, reps, samples = 15, warmup = 5) {
  for (i in seq_len(warmup)) fn()
  gpu_sync()
  t <- vapply(seq_len(samples), function(i) {
    gc(verbose = FALSE)
    t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
    for (j in seq_len(reps)) fn()
    gpu_sync()
    (proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0) / reps
  }, numeric(1))
  median(t)
}

small <- tbl_gpu(data.frame(x = runif(1000), y = runif(1000)), lazy = FALSE)
1e3 * per_call(function() mutate(small, z = x * 2 + y), reps = 200)

big <- data.frame(x = runif(1e6), y = runif(1e6), k = sample.int(100L, 1e6, TRUE))
lz <- tbl_gpu(big, lazy = TRUE)
1e3 * per_call(function() {
  lz |> filter(x > 0.1) |> mutate(z = x * y) |>
    group_by(k) |> summarise(s = sum(z)) |> collect()
}, reps = 10)
rm(small, lz, big)

# README-scale workflow: 25M rows x 6 columns (about 1 GB on the GPU).
n <- 25e6
taxi <- data.frame(
  VendorID = sample(1:4, n, replace = TRUE),
  payment_type = sample(1:5, n, replace = TRUE),
  fare_amount = pmax(2.5, rnorm(n, mean = 13, sd = 10)),
  tip_amount = pmax(0, rnorm(n, mean = 2.5, sd = 3)),
  tolls_amount = runif(n, 0, 15),
  trip_distance = pmax(0.1, rexp(n, rate = 0.3)))
tg <- tbl_gpu(taxi, lazy = TRUE)
rm(taxi); gc()
1e3 * per_call(function() {
  tg |> filter(fare_amount > 0, trip_distance > 0) |>
    mutate(fare_per_mile = fare_amount / trip_distance) |>
    group_by(VendorID, payment_type) |>
    summarise(avg_fare_per_mile = mean(fare_per_mile),
              avg_tip = mean(tip_amount), .groups = "drop") |>
    collect()
}, reps = 3, samples = 9, warmup = 2)
rm(tg)

# Held memory for a table of n doubles (1.25e8 = 1 GB, 3.75e8 = 3 GB).
held <- function(n) {
  host <- data.frame(a = runif(n))
  gpu_gc()
  free0 <- gpu_memory_state()$free_bytes   # the starting point
  g <- tbl_gpu(host, lazy = FALSE)
  gpu_sync()
  rm(g); gc(); gc()
  gpu_sync()
  after_gc_sync <- free0 - gpu_memory_state()$free_bytes
  gpu_gc()
  s <- gpu_memory_state()
  after_gpu_gc <- free0 - s$free_bytes
  c(after_gc_sync = after_gc_sync, after_gpu_gc = after_gpu_gc,
    pool_bytes = s$pool_bytes) / 1e9
}
held(1.25e8)
held(3.75e8)
```
